summary.text: Elastic-rebound theory explains how an earthquake releases energy: rocks across a fault slowly bend under stress, then rupture and snap back almost to their original shape.
While a fault is locked, its two sides keep moving slowly in different directions, so elastic strain builds in the nearby rock, perhaps a few centimeters per year.
Harry Fielding Reid drew the idea from ground movement before the 1906 San Francisco earthquake, and later GPS measurements largely support it.

items.prompt: A straight road is built at right angles across a locked fault. As the years pass, what happens to the road near the fault before any quake?

options.label: It slowly bends out of line
It stays perfectly straight
It slowly sinks into the ground
It cracks into many small pieces

items.explain: The fault's overall motion makes rock across the locked section deform elastically, carrying the road out of line with it.

items.prompt: You bend a plastic ruler between your hands until it slips free and springs straight. Which part of an earthquake does that mimic?

options.label: Magma rising up under the crust
Rocks springing back as the fault ruptures
Rock slowly melting along the fault
Plates sliding smoothly with no friction

items.explain: Strained rocks rupture along the fault and snap back almost to their original shape, releasing stored energy.

items.prompt: When the strained rock along a fault finally lets go, where does its stored energy go?

options.label: All of it into seismic waves
All of it into melting the rock
Into heat, rock changes and seismic waves
It stays locked in the rock for later

items.explain: The stored energy is released partly as heat, partly in altering the rock, and partly as seismic waves.

items.prompt: Reid's idea came from survey data taken before 1906. How did later evidence from satellites hold up against it?

options.label: It showed faults never store strain
It showed plates do not move at all
It could not measure ground movement
It largely backed up his explanation

items.explain: Later measurements using the global positioning system largely support Reid's theory.

items.prompt: Right after the earthquake, you walk along that once-straight road to where it crosses the fault. What do you find?

options.label: The road surface has shifted at the fault
The road is exactly as it was built
The road has risen into a tall ridge
The road has vanished into a deep pit

items.explain: The sudden snap back of the strained rock shifts the roadway's surface where it crosses the fault.

items.prompt: Along the San Andreas Fault, how much ground bending did Reid find over the 50 years before the 1906 quake?

options.label: About 3.2 centimeters
About 3.2 meters
About 32 meters
About 320 meters

items.explain: Reid found evidence of 3.2 meters of bending over those 50 years.
